ideas.title: Mechanism-Conditioned Belief-State Synthesis Planning with Correlated Incompatibility Variables
ideas.motivation: AI will redefine the future of chemistry only when it can propose multi-step syntheses that chemists can trust under scarce, noisy, and biased experimental data. Current models have improved isolated tasks, including template-free retrosynthesis and reaction prediction [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3206796875), mechanism-driven interpretable retrosynthesis [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600), chemistry-aware bond-change outcome prediction [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737), and few-shot selectivity prediction for asymmetric catalysis [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). However, these approaches still mostly score single steps or aggregate route scores through a generic independent-step conjunction of per-step probabilities. Real routes fail through latent shared mechanistic incompatibilities, protecting-group/chemoselectivity states, catalyst poisoning, stereochemical erosion, and correlated side-reaction risks that propagate across steps. A route can have high per-step scores but fail because a hidden condition created in one step invalidates a later step. This idea therefore transfers belief-state planning under uncertainty from probabilistic planning [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W7048571973) and continuous-to-symbolic uncertainty bridging from neuro-symbolic reasoning [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7106207643) to create a synthesis planner that represents, propagates, and reduces mechanism-level route uncertainty rather than only improving single-step predictors.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve unreliable multi-step AI synthesis planning caused by uncalibrated, step-independent uncertainty; it can be divided into 5 parts: a frozen step-prediction layer, a mechanistic incompatibility latent graph, a neuro-symbolic belief updater, a correlated route-risk planner, and a diagnostic experiment selector.

proposed_method.name: Frozen chemistry perception layer
proposed_method.description: Keep existing chemistry predictors fixed so that the first experimental phase tests only the proposed planning mechanism. Candidate retrosynthetic disconnections are generated by a template-free graph-to-sequence retrosynthesis model [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3206796875) or a mechanism-driven retrosynthesis framework [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600). Reaction outcome feasibility is scored with a chemistry-aware bond-change model [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737), and selectivity-sensitive steps are scored with a meta-learning model for asymmetric catalysis [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). The predictor outputs are calibrated with ensembles or conformal prediction, but the predictors are not retrained during the primary hypothesis test.

proposed_method.name: Mechanistic incompatibility latent graph
proposed_method.description: Construct a discrete latent-variable graph over hidden mechanistic states, including reaction-center electron-flow compatibility, protecting-group occupancy, chemoselectivity masks, catalyst-poison presence, stereochemical integrity, and side-reaction susceptibility. Variables are attached to molecular fragments and persist across retrosynthetic steps. Edges encode mechanism-induced dependencies, such as a deprotection revealing a nucleophile that later competes with an electrophile, a residual base that erodes stereochemistry, or a sulfur-containing impurity that poisons a later asymmetric hydrogenation catalyst. This structured representation extends mechanism-aware retrosynthesis [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600) and chemistry-aware bond-change modeling [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737) from single-step plausibility to route-level correlated failure modeling.

proposed_method.name: Neuro-symbolic belief updater
proposed_method.description: Convert continuous predictor probabilities and uncertainty estimates into likelihoods over the discrete mechanistic variables, then update posterior beliefs after each observed or diagnostic result. This adapts neuro-symbolic bridging of uncertain continuous perception and discrete symbolic planning [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W7106207643). The continuous layer contains predictor scores for feasibility, yield, and selectivity, while the symbolic layer contains mechanistic predicates, protecting-group states, chemoselectivity constraints, and route feasibility constraints. The output is a route-level belief state rather than a single point estimate.

proposed_method.name: Correlated route-risk planner
proposed_method.description: Score each candidate route by marginalizing route success over the mechanistic latent graph instead of multiplying independent step probabilities. Use a fixed mechanism-conditioned risk objective, such as CVaR over latent incompatibility factors, purification-aware yield risk, and enantioselectivity-tail constraints. This adapts probabilistic planning under uncertainty [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W7048571973) to retrosynthetic search and allows the planner to penalize routes whose steps share hidden failure causes, even when each step appears locally plausible.

proposed_method.name: Diagnostic experiment selector
proposed_method.description: When route uncertainty is dominated by a small set of latent mechanistic variables, propose minimal diagnostic experiments, such as a small-scale test reaction, a protecting-group stability assay, a catalyst compatibility check, or an analytical stereochemical probe. Select diagnostics by expected value of information for route utility, then update the belief state and replan. This makes uncertainty reduction target mechanism-level feasibility rather than generic outcome observation, following probabilistic decision-theoretic planning under uncertainty [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W7048571973).

analogy_mapping.inspiration: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty: Bridging Continuous Perception and Discrete Symbolic Planning
analogy_mapping.concept: Explicit propagation of uncertainty from continuous perception into discrete symbolic planning with constraint-aware reasoning
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Reaction predictor probabilities and calibrated uncertainty estimates are treated as uncertain continuous perception, while mechanistic incompatibility variables, protecting-group states, chemoselectivity constraints, and route rules form the discrete symbolic planning layer. The planner propagates predictor uncertainty into route-level symbolic feasibility constraints.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Learning and Optimizing Probabilistic Models for Planning under Uncertainty
analogy_mapping.concept: Belief-state planning, probabilistic action/outcome models, and value-of-information decision making under uncertainty
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Multi-step synthesis is treated as a partially observable sequential decision problem. The system maintains a posterior belief over hidden mechanistic incompatibilities, ranks routes by expected utility and risk, and selects diagnostic experiments that maximally reduce uncertainty about mechanism-level feasibility.

experiment_plan: State the primary hypothesis: propagating route uncertainty through a mechanistically structured latent-variable graph increases selection of feasible routes compared with step-independent uncertainty propagation, when predictors, candidate routes, risk objective, and compute budget are held fixed.

Build a fixed evaluation set. Use one frozen retrosynthesis predictor to generate five candidate routes for 300 held-out targets. For each step, obtain frozen feasibility, yield, and selectivity scores from chemistry-aware and meta-learning predictors where applicable. Have three expert chemists, blinded to model uncertainty scores, label overall route feasibility and mechanistic failure causes, including protecting-group, chemoselectivity, catalyst-poisoning, and stereochemical issues.

Implement five uncertainty-propagation variants: predictor-only independent product; independent product plus mechanism feature penalties; proposed correlated mechanistic belief graph; randomized dependency graph with matched variable and edge counts; and unstructured heuristic mixture of step probabilities and mechanistic risk scores. Use the same calibrated predictor outputs, same route candidates, same mechanism-conditioned CVaR objective, and same top-k selection rule for all variants.

Evaluate the primary factor with one-factor-at-a-time comparison. The only varied factor is the uncertainty dependency structure. Metrics are top-10 route failure rate, AUPRC for feasible routes, Brier score, expected calibration error, and route-length-normalized success. Pre-register a success criterion of at least 10 percent relative reduction in top-10 failure rate versus the best non-structured control with paired bootstrap p < 0.05.

Rule out trivial confounders. Match route length and molecular complexity distributions; include route length as a covariate; equalize wall-clock and inference budgets; verify expert labels are not generated from the same rules used to build the latent graph by using blinded independent annotations; test a randomized latent graph; and confirm that gains persist when the frozen predictor is replaced by an alternative template-free predictor.

Ablate active components. Compare predictor-only, mechanistic variables without edges, edges with random variables, full mechanistic graph, and full graph with diagnostic selection disabled. This isolates whether the effect comes from structured mechanistic dependencies rather than added features, added parameters, or extra computation.

Phase 2, after the core hypothesis is confirmed: test diagnostic experiment selection. Simulate diagnostics by revealing expert-annotated latent states or by running small oracle assays in a partner laboratory. Compare value-of-information diagnostic selection to random diagnostics and highest-step-uncertainty diagnostics under fixed budgets of one, two, and three diagnostics per route.

Phase 3, after diagnostics: expand scope to new reaction classes and few-shot predictors, including asymmetric catalysis and Diels-Alder chemistry, and add multi-objective constraints for cost, safety, step count, and sustainability. Evaluate whether the mechanism-conditioned belief state maintains advantage under distribution shift and scarce data.

Optional prospective validation: send top-ranked and control routes to an automated synthesis platform for a small prospective set, recording step success, yield, selectivity, and failure causes. Use these results to update beliefs and test whether prospective failure prediction generalizes beyond retrospective expert labels.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
*(For chronological coherence, I treat the 2021 graph-to-sequence paper as Paper 0, the 2024 Diels–Alder/NERF paper as Paper 1, and the 2025 meta-learning paper as Paper 2. The supplied subgraph is a shallow citation neighborhood, so the progression is inferred from the evolution of problem framing rather than from long explicit predecessor chains.)*

Paper 0 to Paper 1:  
The 2021 work, **“Permutation invariant graph-to-sequence model for template-free retrosynthesis and reaction prediction,”** represents the phase in which AI for chemistry began moving away from purely text-based SMILES-to-SMILES translation and template-dependent rules toward **graph-based, end-to-end molecular reasoning**. Its core contribution is to treat molecules as graphs and retrosynthesis/reaction prediction as a graph-to-sequence translation problem, with permutation invariance helping the model respect the fact that atoms and bonds can be represented in multiple equivalent orders. This matters because it makes reaction prediction more chemically natural and more scalable than hand-authored templates.  

The transition to the 2024 paper, **“Data-Efficient, Chemistry-Aware Machine Learning Predictions of Diels–Alder Reaction Outcomes,”** reflects a response to a key limitation of that earlier paradigm: generic learned translation models can still be data-hungry and may not explicitly encode the chemical logic of bond breaking and bond formation. The 2024 NERF model shifts the emphasis from broad sequence/graph translation to **chemistry-aware reaction modeling**, explicitly mimicking bonding changes during reactions. The concrete advance is a move from “learn the transformation statistically” to “learn the transformation while respecting reaction mechanics,” enabling more accurate and data-efficient predictions for Diels–Alder outcomes. This is important because it shows that embedding chemical structure and mechanism into the model can reduce dependence on very large datasets and improve chemical plausibility.

Paper 1 to Paper 2:  
The 2024 NERF paper demonstrates that mechanism-aware representations can improve data efficiency, but it remains largely focused on a specific reaction class and does not fully solve the broader problem of making reliable predictions when experimental data are scarce. The 2025 paper, **“A meta-learning approach for selectivity prediction in asymmetric catalysis,”** advances the field by shifting from single-task supervised learning to **meta-learning / few-shot learning**. Its core contribution is to use literature-derived data to learn shared reaction features, then apply that learned prior to new asymmetric catalytic reactions with only a small number of examples.  

This transition matters because it targets a harder and more practically valuable problem: **selectivity prediction**, especially enantioselectivity in transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric reactions. In drug discovery and fine chemical synthesis, selecting the correct stereochemical outcome is often as important as predicting that a reaction can occur. The 2025 work therefore expands the research focus from reaction feasibility or product prediction toward **high-value decision-making in early-stage reaction development**, where data are limited and experimental screening is expensive. The use of prototypical networks and few-shot learning signals a shift from “train one large model on one reaction family” toward “learn how to learn new reaction behaviors quickly.”

Key Turning Points:  
- **From template-based chemistry to learned graph-to-sequence retrosynthesis:** The 2021 paper marks a shift from hand-crafted retrosynthetic rules and SMILES translation toward permutation-invariant graph models that can learn transformations directly from data. This established the feasibility of end-to-end AI-assisted synthesis planning.  
- **From generic pattern learning to chemistry-aware bond-change modeling:** The 2024 NERF paper is a turning point because it explicitly encodes bonding changes, showing that chemical mechanism awareness can improve accuracy and data efficiency. This reflects a broader move toward models that are not only statistically powerful but also chemically grounded.  
- **From large-data supervised prediction to low-data meta-learning for selectivity:** The 2025 meta-learning paper marks a shift toward data-efficient learning in high-value, data-sparse settings. Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric catalysis with few examples is a major step toward practical AI support for reaction discovery.  
- **Toward mechanism-driven, interpretable pathway planning:** The seed paper, **MechRetro**, can be read as a synthesis of these trends: it seeks to combine graph learning, chemical mechanism, interpretability, and retrosynthetic pathway planning. This indicates a field-level move from isolated prediction tasks toward actionable, explainable synthesis design.

Recurring Limitations:  
- **Dependence on large or highly curated reaction datasets:** Across the lineage, a recurring problem is that many ML models require substantial amounts of reaction data, while new reactions, catalysts, and selectivity problems often have only limited experimental examples.  
- **Limited generalization across reaction classes:** The 2024 model improves data efficiency for Diels–Alder reactions, and the 2025 model improves few-shot learning for asymmetric hydrogenation, but both suggest that strong performance may still be tied to relatively narrow chemical domains. Broad, cross-reaction generalization remains difficult.  
- **Difficulty predicting selectivity and complex reaction outcomes:** Retrosynthesis and product prediction are already challenging, but selectivity—especially enantioselectivity—introduces subtler stereochemical, conformational, and catalyst-dependent effects that are not fully resolved by standard graph or sequence models.  
- **Tension between generic end-to-end learning and chemically constrained modeling:** The 2021 graph-to-sequence approach emphasizes flexible learned translation, while the 2024 chemistry-aware model emphasizes mechanistic fidelity. The field has not yet fully reconciled broad generality with deep chemical constraint satisfaction.  
- **Insufficient integration with full synthesis planning:** Reaction outcome prediction, retrosynthesis, condition recommendation, yield prediction, and route feasibility are often treated as separate problems. A fully useful AI chemistry system would need to integrate all of these into a coherent planning workflow.  
- **Interpretability remains incomplete:** Even as models become more chemistry-aware, there is still a gap between predictive performance and explanations that chemists can trust, verify, and use to guide experiments.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- **Mechanistically constrained retrosynthesis and reaction prediction:** A major open problem is to build models that not only propose plausible retrosynthetic disconnections but also obey mechanistic, electronic, thermodynamic, and kinetic constraints. Current systems can generate chemically reasonable-looking routes that may still fail under real reaction conditions.  
- **Uncertainty-quantified synthesis planning:** AI models need calibrated confidence estimates for retrosynthetic steps, reaction outcomes, yields, and selectivity. Without reliable uncertainty quantification, chemists cannot know when a proposed route is robust or when the model is extrapolating dangerously.  
- **Generalizable few-shot learning across diverse chemistry:** Meta-learning and data-efficient models show promise, but they are often demonstrated on narrow reaction families. A key unsolved problem is to create transferable models that can rapidly adapt to new reaction classes, catalysts, substrates, and selectivity regimes without extensive retraining.  
- **Unified prediction of feasibility, yield, selectivity, conditions, and route practicality:** Most current models address one subproblem at a time. The field still lacks a unified scientific framework that jointly predicts whether a reaction works, what product forms, in what yield, with what selectivity, under which conditions, and whether it is practical in a multi-step synthesis.  
- **Interpretable causal chemical reasoning:** Interpretability must move beyond attention weights or feature importance toward mechanistic explanations: why a bond forms, why a catalyst favors one enantiomer, why a side reaction dominates, or why a route may fail. This requires causal, mechanism-aware representations rather than purely correlational models.  
- **Learning from noisy, biased, and negative experimental data:** Chemical literature data are often incomplete, biased toward successful reactions, and inconsistent in reporting conditions. A major scientific challenge is to build models that can learn robustly from noisy positive data, infer useful information from missing or negative results, and handle experimental uncertainty.  
- **Closed-loop integration with autonomous experimentation:** AI will truly redefine chemistry when it can plan experiments, execute them through automated platforms, observe outcomes, and update its models. The scientific gap is not just prediction but closed-loop optimization under real-world constraints such as safety, cost, reagent availability, and scalability.  
- **Multi-objective route optimization for real-world synthesis:** Future chemistry AI must optimize not only for route feasibility but also for cost, sustainability, toxicity, step count, purification burden, energy usage, and regulatory constraints. This requires scientific advances in multi-objective molecular and process optimization, not just reaction prediction.

[ABSTRACT] Transition metal-catalyzed asymmetric reactions are of high contemporary importance in organic synthesis. Recently, machine learning (ML) has shown promise in accelerating the development of newer catalytic protocols. However, the need for large amount of experimental data can present a bottleneck for implementing ML models. Here, we propose a meta-learning workflow that can harness the literature-derived data to extract shared reaction features and requires only a few examples to predict the outcome of new reactions. Prototypical networks are used as a meta-learning method to predict the enantioselectivity of asymmetric hydrogenation of olefins. This meta-learning model consistently provides significant performance improvement over other popular ML methods such as random forests and graph neural networks. The performance of our meta-model is analyzed with varying sizes of training examples to demonstrate its utility even with limited data. A good model performance on an out-of-sample test set further indicates the general applicability of our approach. We believe this work will provide a leap forward in identifying promising reactions in the early phases of reaction development when minimal data is available.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
*(For chronological coherence, I treat the 2021 graph-to-sequence paper as Paper 0, the 2024 Diels–Alder/NERF paper as Paper 1, and the 2025 meta-learning paper as Paper 2. The supplied subgraph is a shallow citation neighborhood, so the progression is inferred from the evolution of problem framing rather than from long explicit predecessor chains.)*

Paper 0 to Paper 1:  
The 2021 work, **“Permutation invariant graph-to-sequence model for template-free retrosynthesis and reaction prediction,”** represents the phase in which AI for chemistry began moving away from purely text-based SMILES-to-SMILES translation and template-dependent rules toward **graph-based, end-to-end molecular reasoning**. Its core contribution is to treat molecules as graphs and retrosynthesis/reaction prediction as a graph-to-sequence translation problem, with permutation invariance helping the model respect the fact that atoms and bonds can be represented in multiple equivalent orders. This matters because it makes reaction prediction more chemically natural and more scalable than hand-authored templates.  

The transition to the 2024 paper, **“Data-Efficient, Chemistry-Aware Machine Learning Predictions of Diels–Alder Reaction Outcomes,”** reflects a response to a key limitation of that earlier paradigm: generic learned translation models can still be data-hungry and may not explicitly encode the chemical logic of bond breaking and bond formation. The 2024 NERF model shifts the emphasis from broad sequence/graph translation to **chemistry-aware reaction modeling**, explicitly mimicking bonding changes during reactions. The concrete advance is a move from “learn the transformation statistically” to “learn the transformation while respecting reaction mechanics,” enabling more accurate and data-efficient predictions for Diels–Alder outcomes. This is important because it shows that embedding chemical structure and mechanism into the model can reduce dependence on very large datasets and improve chemical plausibility.

Paper 1 to Paper 2:  
The 2024 NERF paper demonstrates that mechanism-aware representations can improve data efficiency, but it remains largely focused on a specific reaction class and does not fully solve the broader problem of making reliable predictions when experimental data are scarce. The 2025 paper, **“A meta-learning approach for selectivity prediction in asymmetric catalysis,”** advances the field by shifting from single-task supervised learning to **meta-learning / few-shot learning**. Its core contribution is to use literature-derived data to learn shared reaction features, then apply that learned prior to new asymmetric catalytic reactions with only a small number of examples.  

This transition matters because it targets a harder and more practically valuable problem: **selectivity prediction**, especially enantioselectivity in transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric reactions. In drug discovery and fine chemical synthesis, selecting the correct stereochemical outcome is often as important as predicting that a reaction can occur. The 2025 work therefore expands the research focus from reaction feasibility or product prediction toward **high-value decision-making in early-stage reaction development**, where data are limited and experimental screening is expensive. The use of prototypical networks and few-shot learning signals a shift from “train one large model on one reaction family” toward “learn how to learn new reaction behaviors quickly.”

Key Turning Points:  
- **From template-based chemistry to learned graph-to-sequence retrosynthesis:** The 2021 paper marks a shift from hand-crafted retrosynthetic rules and SMILES translation toward permutation-invariant graph models that can learn transformations directly from data. This established the feasibility of end-to-end AI-assisted synthesis planning.  
- **From generic pattern learning to chemistry-aware bond-change modeling:** The 2024 NERF paper is a turning point because it explicitly encodes bonding changes, showing that chemical mechanism awareness can improve accuracy and data efficiency. This reflects a broader move toward models that are not only statistically powerful but also chemically grounded.  
- **From large-data supervised prediction to low-data meta-learning for selectivity:** The 2025 meta-learning paper marks a shift toward data-efficient learning in high-value, data-sparse settings. Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric catalysis with few examples is a major step toward practical AI support for reaction discovery.  
- **Toward mechanism-driven, interpretable pathway planning:** The seed paper, **MechRetro**, can be read as a synthesis of these trends: it seeks to combine graph learning, chemical mechanism, interpretability, and retrosynthetic pathway planning. This indicates a field-level move from isolated prediction tasks toward actionable, explainable synthesis design.

Recurring Limitations:  
- **Dependence on large or highly curated reaction datasets:** Across the lineage, a recurring problem is that many ML models require substantial amounts of reaction data, while new reactions, catalysts, and selectivity problems often have only limited experimental examples.  
- **Limited generalization across reaction classes:** The 2024 model improves data efficiency for Diels–Alder reactions, and the 2025 model improves few-shot learning for asymmetric hydrogenation, but both suggest that strong performance may still be tied to relatively narrow chemical domains. Broad, cross-reaction generalization remains difficult.  
- **Difficulty predicting selectivity and complex reaction outcomes:** Retrosynthesis and product prediction are already challenging, but selectivity—especially enantioselectivity—introduces subtler stereochemical, conformational, and catalyst-dependent effects that are not fully resolved by standard graph or sequence models.  
- **Tension between generic end-to-end learning and chemically constrained modeling:** The 2021 graph-to-sequence approach emphasizes flexible learned translation, while the 2024 chemistry-aware model emphasizes mechanistic fidelity. The field has not yet fully reconciled broad generality with deep chemical constraint satisfaction.  
- **Insufficient integration with full synthesis planning:** Reaction outcome prediction, retrosynthesis, condition recommendation, yield prediction, and route feasibility are often treated as separate problems. A fully useful AI chemistry system would need to integrate all of these into a coherent planning workflow.  
- **Interpretability remains incomplete:** Even as models become more chemistry-aware, there is still a gap between predictive performance and explanations that chemists can trust, verify, and use to guide experiments.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- **Mechanistically constrained retrosynthesis and reaction prediction:** A major open problem is to build models that not only propose plausible retrosynthetic disconnections but also obey mechanistic, electronic, thermodynamic, and kinetic constraints. Current systems can generate chemically reasonable-looking routes that may still fail under real reaction conditions.  
- **Uncertainty-quantified synthesis planning:** AI models need calibrated confidence estimates for retrosynthetic steps, reaction outcomes, yields, and selectivity. Without reliable uncertainty quantification, chemists cannot know when a proposed route is robust or when the model is extrapolating dangerously.  
- **Generalizable few-shot learning across diverse chemistry:** Meta-learning and data-efficient models show promise, but they are often demonstrated on narrow reaction families. A key unsolved problem is to create transferable models that can rapidly adapt to new reaction classes, catalysts, substrates, and selectivity regimes without extensive retraining.  
- **Unified prediction of feasibility, yield, selectivity, conditions, and route practicality:** Most current models address one subproblem at a time. The field still lacks a unified scientific framework that jointly predicts whether a reaction works, what product forms, in what yield, with what selectivity, under which conditions, and whether it is practical in a multi-step synthesis.  
- **Interpretable causal chemical reasoning:** Interpretability must move beyond attention weights or feature importance toward mechanistic explanations: why a bond forms, why a catalyst favors one enantiomer, why a side reaction dominates, or why a route may fail. This requires causal, mechanism-aware representations rather than purely correlational models.  
- **Learning from noisy, biased, and negative experimental data:** Chemical literature data are often incomplete, biased toward successful reactions, and inconsistent in reporting conditions. A major scientific challenge is to build models that can learn robustly from noisy positive data, infer useful information from missing or negative results, and handle experimental uncertainty.  
- **Closed-loop integration with autonomous experimentation:** AI will truly redefine chemistry when it can plan experiments, execute them through automated platforms, observe outcomes, and update its models. The scientific gap is not just prediction but closed-loop optimization under real-world constraints such as safety, cost, reagent availability, and scalability.  
- **Multi-objective route optimization for real-world synthesis:** Future chemistry AI must optimize not only for route feasibility but also for cost, sustainability, toxicity, step count, purification burden, energy usage, and regulatory constraints. This requires scientific advances in multi-objective molecular and process optimization, not just reaction prediction.

- Novelty feedback from the previous round: Idea 1: Mechanism-Conditioned Belief-State Synthesis Planning with Correlated Incompatibility Variables
Novelty level: medium
Justification: The closest existing combination among the provided references is MechRetro paired with the template-free graph-to-sequence retrosynthesis model, the asymmetric-catalysis selectivity predictor, and the Diels-Alder outcome predictor. MechRetro already incorporates chemical mechanism into graph-based retrosynthesis and pathway planning, while the other references supply step-level feasibility, outcome, or selectivity predictions. The proposed idea goes beyond these works by freezing such predictors and adding a route-level latent graph of mechanistic incompatibility variables, a belief-state updater that converts calibrated predictor uncertainty into posterior beliefs, correlated risk-sensitive route scoring, and value-of-information diagnostic experiment selection. This route-level correlated-failure formulation is not directly present in the key references and is framed as a testable hypothesis comparing structured mechanistic dependency propagation with independent step-probability aggregation. However, the core contribution is largely a transfer of established probabilistic planning and neuro-symbolic uncertainty-bridging concepts to synthesis planning, using already-known predictor components. The advance is therefore meaningful but more integrative than fundamentally new, supporting a medium novelty rating.
Improvement suggestions: Sharpen the conceptual advance by defining a causal semantics for latent incompatibility variables: specify interventions such as protecting-group changes, catalyst substitution, purification operations, or workup modifications, and model counterfactual route outcomes so the planner predicts the effect of mechanistic repairs rather than only flagging correlated failure risks.; Make the latent mechanistic graph learnable or identifiable rather than primarily hand-designed: infer variables and dependency edges from route-failure data, expert annotations, or mechanism databases using constraints that distinguish true mechanistic dependencies from spurious correlations among step scores.; Introduce a chemistry-specific belief-revision mechanism with formal properties, such as constraint-satisfaction over protecting-group occupancy, chemoselectivity masks, and catalyst-poison invariants with monotonicity or consistency guarantees, instead of relying mainly on generic probabilistic planning machinery.

ideas.title: Causal Mechanism-State Model Predictive Planning for Repairable Retrosynthesis
ideas.motivation: AI can redefine chemistry only if planning systems move from isolated step prediction to robust, repairable multi-step synthesis. Template-free graph-to-sequence models showed that retrosynthesis and reaction prediction can be learned end-to-end [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3206796875). Mechanism-aware bond-change models improve data efficiency and chemical plausibility for reaction outcomes [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737), and meta-learning addresses scarce selectivity data in asymmetric catalysis [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). MechRetro further demonstrates that chemical mechanism can make retrosynthesis and pathway planning more interpretable [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600). However, current planners still lack a causal intervention semantics for route repair: they do not predict how changing a protecting group, catalyst, purification, or workup will alter correlated mechanistic incompatibilities, nor do they plan under calibrated uncertainty. Predictive-control research provides the needed mechanism: learning-based model predictive control enables safe exploration with learned dynamics and explicit constraints [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2791704483), while the state-space versus direct multi-step predictor comparison motivates a controlled test of recursive mechanistic state models for sequential chemistry decisions [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4224330578).
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve uncertainty-brittle multi-step synthesis planning by making route repair an explicit causal control problem; it can be divided into 4 parts: a causal mechanism-state representation, a learnable incompatibility-graph learner, an intervention-conditioned transition model, and a receding-horizon constrained repair planner. The primary hypothesis is that, with frozen step predictors and matched model capacity, a recursive mechanism-state model with intervention variables predicts counterfactual route repairs and achieves higher validated route success than a direct multi-step route predictor or independent step aggregation. The mechanism is tested first by varying only the state-transition structure while holding data, predictors, constraints, and compute fixed.

proposed_method.name: Causal mechanism-state representation with formal belief revision
proposed_method.description: Represent each route as a trajectory of mechanistic state vectors s_t over molecular graphs, protecting-group occupancy, chemoselectivity masks, catalyst-condition compatibility, poison or impurity accumulation, and calibrated outcome beliefs. Repair actions are explicit causal interventions do(a), including reaction step, protecting-group change, catalyst substitution, purification, workup, or condition adjustment. A projection operator updates beliefs by enforcing chemical invariants: conflicting protecting groups cannot occupy the same site, catalyst-poison load is monotone unless removed by an explicit purification intervention, chemoselectivity masks remain disjoint, and bond changes must satisfy mechanism-enabled preconditions. This converts generic uncertainty into a chemistry-specific belief revision process rather than a hand-written failure flag, and it builds on mechanism-driven retrosynthetic graph learning [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600).

proposed_method.name: Learnable mechanistic incompatibility graph
proposed_method.description: Infer directed latent dependencies among state variables, reaction steps, and repair interventions from route outcomes, weak literature labels, expert annotations, and mechanism priors. The graph learner is constrained by temporal order, sparsity, and intervention identifiability so that edges represent testable causal dependencies such as catalyst poisoning, protecting-group lability, or chemoselectivity conflict, rather than only correlation. In data-sparse reaction families, the learner can reuse shared reaction features through meta-learning style adaptation [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). In the primary controlled phase the graph is planted; in later phases it is learned and compared against expert or planted graphs.

proposed_method.name: Intervention-conditioned transition and calibration model
proposed_method.description: Use frozen step-level predictors as observation models: template-free graph-to-sequence retrosynthesis and reaction prediction [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3206796875), chemistry-aware bond-change outcome prediction [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737), selectivity prediction for low-data asymmetric catalysis [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348), and mechanism-driven retrosynthetic disconnection scoring [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600). Train a compact transition function f_theta(s_t, do(a)) to predict the next mechanistic state, product distribution, yield-selectivity distribution, and constraint-violation probabilities. The recursive formulation is deliberately contrasted with direct multi-step endpoint prediction, following the predictive-control distinction between state-space models and direct multi-step predictors [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4224330578).

proposed_method.name: Safe receding-horizon repair planner
proposed_method.description: Borrow learning-based model predictive control from control engineering to plan repair interventions over a finite horizon. At each decision point, the planner samples candidate action sequences, propagates them through the transition model, and selects the first action that maximizes expected route success while satisfying chance constraints on invariant violations and uncertainty thresholds. Safe exploration prioritizes repairs that are informative but unlikely to violate mechanistic feasibility, selectivity, or compatibility constraints. This adaptation gives synthesis planning a constrained sequential-decision structure rather than a one-shot route ranking [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2791704483).

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Learning-based Model Predictive Control for Safe Exploration and Reinforcement Learning
analogy_mapping.concept: Receding-horizon constrained planning with learned dynamics and safe exploration under uncertainty
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Used as the synthesis repair planner: candidate reaction and repair interventions are evaluated over a rolling horizon with chance constraints on mechanistic invariant violations and calibrated uncertainty.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: State space models vs. multi-step predictors in predictive control: Are state space models complicating safe data-driven designs?
analogy_mapping.concept: Explicit recursive state-space modeling versus direct multi-step prediction for sequential decision systems
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Used to define the primary falsifiable comparison between a recursive causal mechanism-state transition model and a direct multi-step route-outcome predictor under matched data and capacity.

experiment_plan: Primary hypothesis: With frozen step-level predictors and matched capacity and data, a recursive causal mechanism-state transition model with explicit repair interventions will produce lower counterfactual repair error and higher route success than independent step aggregation and a direct multi-step route predictor.

Construct a controlled semi-synthetic benchmark by generating candidate routes for drug-like targets using mechanism-driven retrosynthesis [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4308632600) and template-free reaction prediction [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3206796875), then overlay known causal incompatibilities such as protecting-group conflicts, catalyst poisons, and chemoselectivity violations with simulated yields and selectivities using chemistry-aware outcome models [Author et al., 2024](https://openalex.org/W4392515737) and selectivity models [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). Hold route sets, predictor outputs, noise level, and data budget fixed.

Train three route-repair scorers that share the same frozen predictor features and training examples: independent step aggregation, direct multi-step endpoint predictor, and the causal mechanism-state model. Vary only the state-transition structure; match parameter count, optimizer, training tokens, and candidate-repair pool.

Add mechanism controls: randomized incompatibility graph with the same state dimension, mechanism-state model without intervention variables, late-fusion physical mixture of frozen predictors, and each frozen predictor alone. These separate structured causal mechanism from extra capacity, constraint filtering, or predictor ensembling.

Evaluate primary outcomes: counterfactual repair prediction error on held-out interventions, calibration using Brier score and expected calibration error, route success under simulated execution, and recovery of planted causal edges. Rule out confounders by stratifying by route length and reaction class, using leave-one-reaction-class-out splits, verifying matched compute, and testing whether randomized constraints remove the advantage.

Only if the primary hypothesis is supported, vary data scarcity and noise to test robustness: reduce labeled route failures to 1%, 5%, and 10%, add biased positive-only reporting, and compare with meta-learning adaptation [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4409453348). Keep the winning state-transition structure fixed while varying data regime.

Phase 2: replace the planted incompatibility graph with the learnable graph estimator using expert annotations and weak literature labels; compare learned graph to planted or expert graph using edge AUROC and intervention prediction, while holding transition model and planner fixed.

Phase 3: integrate the validated state model into the model-predictive-control repair planner [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2791704483). Compare against greedy planning and exhaustive route search using the same state model, horizon, candidate pool, and compute. Vary only the chance-constraint threshold to test safe exploration.

Rule out planner confounders: equalize number of rollout evaluations, disable constraint projection in a control, use a direct multi-step predictor inside the same search where possible, and confirm that improvements persist after normalizing by route length and target complexity.

Final translational test: prospective expert-in-the-loop case studies on 20 pharmaceutically relevant targets, where the system proposes routes and repair interventions; measure expert-accepted feasibility, predicted versus literature or experimental outcomes, and number of avoided failed steps.

parsed_json.justification: The closest existing combination is MechRetro together with the cited step-level predictors: template-free retrosynthesis/reaction prediction, chemistry-aware Diels-Alder outcome modeling, and meta-learning selectivity prediction. MechRetro already supplies mechanism-aware, interpretable retrosynthetic pathway planning, while the other references supply plausible frozen predictors for individual reaction outcomes. The proposed idea adds a meaningful layer not present in those references: explicit repair actions as causal interventions, a mechanistic state trajectory with chemistry-specific belief revision, a learnable incompatibility graph, and a receding-horizon model-predictive-control planner. This gives the proposal a testable conceptual claim: recursive intervention-conditioned mechanism-state modeling should outperform independent step aggregation or direct multi-step route prediction for counterfactual repair and route success. However, the novelty is still partly combination-oriented because it largely integrates existing mechanism-aware retrosynthesis components with borrowed MPC and causal-learning machinery, rather than introducing a fundamentally new chemical planning principle. It is therefore not purely combination-only, but its advance is more architectural and formulation-level than deeply mechanistic, supporting a medium rating.
